# Reflection & Learnings

## Challenges & Lessons Learned

Since we lacked access to real customer data, we built our own synthetic dataset: ten personas, their subscriptions, and roughly two thousand synthetic trip legs, varied enough to keep the recommendations meaningful rather than trivially regular. The tariff data is real, drawn from 62 documents of published provider pricing. But the customer side means we were marking our own homework: the engine prices real tariffs correctly against behaviour we designed, with no way to know how it handles a real customer's unexplained Uber every third Friday. Onboarding's provider connection is simulated for the same reason, designed as though it were real so that only the data source would need replacing later.

A separate lesson was how quickly a generative coding assistant let us start building, sometimes before we had worked out where we were going. None of us had built an agentic system before, so we treated the architecture as something to discover by iterating on it rather than settling it upfront. It went through several revisions, and so did the synthetic personas we tested it against. Some of that uncertainty ran deeper: for a while we doubted a deterministic script could substitute for judgement calls at all, since capturing real travel behaviour this way meant committing to simplifying assumptions before we could test whether they would hold up. In hindsight, pinning down the user story and scope more before writing code, or scoping down further to a single transport mode, would have kept the moving parts easier to hold in view. At the same time, we doubt we would have attempted a project this size within one semester without that same assistance.

## Limitations & Next Steps

The tariff data is a snapshot with no mechanism yet for updating prices as provider conditions change, and the synthetic trip data carries a related simplification: each mode's per-trip cost and duration comes from a fixed per-kilometre estimate rather than a real fare structure, so distance-based pricing tiers or time-of-day variation are absent even from the travel history the recommendations are based on. Onboarding's provider connection is likewise simulated, and not every tariff would supply this data on its own regardless: a flat-rate product like the Deutschlandticket has no natural per-trip billing event to track. The system also only analyses and forecasts so far, rather than acting on what it finds: the dashboard already offers controls to switch, cancel, or take up a subscription from the recommendation view, but these do not yet write to the backend, so the portfolio reverts on reload and the only path that actually commits a change is confirming it with the Advisor in chat.

Another limitation concerns the transport data for alternatives the customer never actually used. CO~2~ emissions and travel duration rely on manually defined averages rather than route-specific data, and availability is idealised too: the system never checks whether an alternative is actually serviceable on the customer's routes, treating every subscribed provider as equally reachable rather than modelling how unevenly dense a scooter or car-sharing fleet really is, which is more forgiving in the urban settings the product targets than for someone outside a city, where owning a car is often the only practical option anyway. The multi-criteria scoring is also limited by the problem's structure: within a category the alternatives do not change how a person travels, so emissions and duration are identical and the decision is effectively made on cost, while CO~2~ and flexibility only become decisive across different modes. The system also considers one person at a time, so it supports neither shared households nor employer-funded mobility, nor does its modal comparison extend to on-demand services such as taxis.

Two further limitations concern how much the analysis itself can be trusted. It assumes enough history to be meaningful: a newly onboarded customer with only a few weeks of recorded travel gives the pipeline far less signal than the twelve months used in this evaluation, with no fallback for that shorter horizon. And because the engine's own output serves as the ground truth the baseline is scored against (Chapter 6), the evaluation shows consistency between the two rather than that the engine's recommendations are correct in an absolute sense. A systematic error in the deterministic logic would not surface without an independent ground truth.

Future work could address these limitations in several ways: a real OAuth-based provider connection, starting with the Deutschlandticket, would give the system actual travel data; route-level emissions and duration from a routing service would give the CO~2~ and time axes the resolution manually defined averages cannot; wiring the dashboard's switch/cancel controls into the Advisor's existing confirm-and-apply flow would let a customer act directly instead of going through chat; and extending the evaluation from a single run to rolling time windows would test the product's core claim, that its advice stays correct as behaviour changes. None of this requires redesigning anything: the tariff knowledge base is file-driven, and the scoring engine takes its weights as parameters rather than hard-coding them.
